E01.title: Numerical verification of lambda across all COMPADRE matrices
E01.question: Do two independent algorithms (LAPACK eigendecomposition vs power iteration) agree on lambda for every valid COMPADRE v6.26.3.0 matrix?
E01.hypothesis: Agreement within 1e-6 for >=99% of primitive matrices; disagreements only for imprimitive/reducible matrices.
E01.method: eig vs power iteration; Validation flags
E01.finding: Two independent numerical methods agree; imprimitive matrices need eigen-based lambda (power iteration oscillates).

E02.title: Medicinal-species coverage audit (independent verification of prior claims)
E02.question: How many COMPADRE / Environmental-Demography / PhenObs taxa have documented medicinal use in open checklists, and do the prior-agent claims (>=333, >=68, >=307) replicate?
E02.hypothesis: Counts will be lower than prior claims because open checklists (USDA Duke, Herbolario) replace restricted Kew WCUPS/MPNS; each dataset still exceeds 10 medicinal species with usable outcomes.
E02.data: COMPADRE 6.26.3.0; GBIF backbone; USDA Duke ETHNOBOT; Herbolario; EnvDemog GLMMdata; PhenObs 2019-2023
E02.method: GBIF accepted+true synonyms, manual synonym review, binomial match
E02.finding: All three datasets pass the >=10 medicinal-species threshold; the larger prior counts are not reproduced with open checklists.

E03.title: Flagship reproduction: Nardostachys jatamansi rhizome-harvest experiment
E03.question: Do COMPADRE matrices for Ghimire et al. (2008) reproduce the paper's monotonic decline of lambda with harvest intensity, and through which vital rates?
E03.hypothesis: lambda decreases monotonically with intensity (0-75%); harvest effect acts mainly through survival/growth (stasis+progression) rather than fecundity, consistent with elasticity of a long-lived clonal herb.
E03.data: COMPADRE 244454-244459; Ghimire et al. 2008 (full text, docs/research)
E03.method: eigen-analysis, power check, fixed LTRE by process, Spearman
E03.finding: Ordering identical to the paper and strictly monotonic (Spearman rho=-1.00); each +10% harvest lowers lambda by 0.036. Exact values differ (COMPADRE = 1999-2002 means). LTRE share of |effect|: progression 38%, retrogression 31%, stasis 29%, fecundity 2%: harvest acts through growth/survival and shrinkage of ramet clusters, not seed production.

E04.title: Cross-study synthesis of medicinal-plant harvest contrasts in COMPADRE
E04.question: Across all audited medicinal harvest studies in COMPADRE, does harvest consistently lower deterministic lambda, as the NTFP meta-analysis (Schmidt et al. 2011: pooled 1.04 control vs 0.92 harvest) suggests?
E04.hypothesis: Harvest lowers lambda in most studies, but effects are heterogeneous and weaker in observational (non-randomised) contrasts than in the experimental flagship.
E04.method: per-study delta lambda, design-stratified; permutation tests where >=3 populations per arm
E04.finding: Harvest lowered lambda in 6/8 studies (sign test p=0.29). Only the randomised flagship shows a large effect; observational contrasts are small and confounded with site/period. Generic 'harvest lowers lambda by X' transfer across species is NOT supported.

E05.title: Back-test: can a generic counterfactual removal model (Tier B) predict observed harvest effects?
E05.question: If we had no harvest experiment for Nardostachys, would a simple 'remove fraction h of plants in harvested stages' model applied to the control matrix predict the observed treatment lambdas?
E05.hypothesis: Generic removal models are miscalibrated because rhizome harvest causes partial biomass loss and stage regression rather than death; error will exceed 0.05 in lambda for >=25% intensities.
E05.finding: No generic removal model reproduces the experiment (best MAE 0.068; lethal-all bias -0.226, largest-class-only bias +0.068). Decision rule: Tier-B counterfactuals may be shown only as labelled sensitivity ranges, never as harvest-rate advice.

E06.title: Recovery time and rotation thresholds for Nardostachys (study-matrix extrapolation)
E06.question: Using only the study's own matrices, after how many years does abundance recover from one harvest, and what rest interval keeps the annualised growth rate >= 1 under repeated harvest?
E06.hypothesis: Recovery lengthens with intensity; minimal rotation length increases with intensity; values will NOT match the paper's recovery times (5/17/33 yr) because COMPADRE stores 3-year mean matrices that already include post-harvest recovery.
E06.method: recovery_time, periodic_lambda; sensitivity to control choice (outcrop control vs meadow)
E06.finding: Recovery times are shorter than published (not reproduced) - a known limitation of mean matrices. Rotation thresholds are model extrapolations and depend on which control is used; shown in Simulate as 'study-matrix extrapolation', never as a permitted rotation.

E07.title: Elasticity structure of medicinal taxa by growth form (harvest-vulnerability screening)
E07.question: Do medicinal trees/long-lived perennials have higher survival-stasis elasticity than short-lived herbs, implying adult/organ harvest is riskier?
E07.hypothesis: Median stasis elasticity: trees > perennials > short-lived; fecundity elasticity the reverse (Kruskal-Wallis p<0.05), one value per species (not per matrix).
E07.data: COMPADRE medicinal taxa, unmanipulated mean/pooled matrices passing QC
E07.finding: Median stasis elasticity: woody 0.857, herbaceous perennial 0.486, annual 0.005 (Kruskal-Wallis p=4.3e-12); fecundity elasticity reverses. Used only as a qualitative screening flag for species without harvest experiments; descriptive, species-level, not phylogenetically corrected.

E08.title: PhenObs: is peak flowering of medicinal species predictable across gardens (monitoring calendar)?
E08.question: For medicinal species monitored in >=3 botanical gardens, how much of peak-flowering-day variance is species identity vs garden vs year, and does a species-mean model beat a grand-mean baseline in leave-one-garden-out prediction?
E08.hypothesis: Species explains most variance; species-mean beats grand mean (lower MAE); adding a garden offset improves further. Gardens are not wild populations.
E08.method: variance components via OLS sums of squares; leave-one-garden-out CV
E08.finding: Species identity explains 79% of peak-flowering variance (garden 4%, year 0.4%). Leave-one-garden-out MAE: grand mean 35.5 d, species mean 15.4 d, +garden offset 14.1 d. Published C-score/intensity link: rho=0.14, p=0.025 (weak, same direction). Garden plants, not wild populations: monitoring-window suggestion only.

E09.title: Environmental Demography: reproduce life-history and aridity association with demographic buffering
E09.question: Do life-history axes (LHPC) and climate axes (ClimPC) predict the cumulative stochastic elasticity of variance across 121 populations, as the manuscript reports?
E09.hypothesis: LHPC.1 (survival-reproduction trade-off axis) has a significant association with log cumulative SigElas; ClimPC terms add explanatory power. Non-phylogenetic mixed model is a simplification of the authors' MCMCglmm.
E09.method: linear mixed model (species random intercept) vs LH-only vs null; AIC; medicinal subset
E09.finding: Not replicated for life history: LH1 p=0.34 in a non-phylogenetic mixed model. Climate axes are associated (ClimPC1 p=0.0001, ClimPC2 p=0.0007; AIC 506 -> 486). The authors' phylogenetic MCMCglmm on separate vital-rate elasticities may detect what this simplification misses; treated as contextual, not used for harvest decisions.

E10.title: Habitat suitability: spatial-block vs random CV, climate-4 baseline vs complex models, negative control
E10.question: For medicinal species with sufficient GBIF presences, does a 19-variable model beat a 4-variable climate baseline under spatial-block CV, and how optimistic is random CV?
E10.hypothesis: Random CV overstates AUC relative to 5-degree spatial blocks; complex models gain <0.03 AUC over the baseline under spatial CV; shuffled-label control ~0.5; Nardostachys is suppressed (<100 presences).
E10.method: presence-background; 5-fold random vs 5-degree block CV; AUC/AP
E10.finding: Primula veris: baseline spatial AUC 0.593, best gbm_bio19 0.642, random-CV optimism +0.188, shuffled 0.49, served gbm_bio19 (suppressed) | Arnica montana: baseline spatial AUC 0.715, best gbm_bio19 0.751, random-CV optimism +0.162, shuffled 0.49, served gbm_bio19 (eligible) | Nardostachys jatamansi: baseline spatial AUC 0.773, best logistic_bio19_l2 0.786, random-CV optimism +0.025, shuffled 0.47, served logistic_bio19_l2 (eligible) | Hypothesis check: random-CV optimism confirmed; complex-model gain over baseline Primula +0.049, Arnica +0.036, Nardostachys +0.014; Nardostachys suppression prediction REJECTED (134 presences passed the >=100 rule; small-sample model flagged in UI).

E11.title: JEV study-triage benchmark (rubric-labelled)
E11.question: On papers about medicinal plants, does JEV classify what a study measured (harvest effect on this species / other species / demography without harvest / other topic) better than keyword rules, and is its confidence calibrated?
E11.hypothesis: JEV macro-F1 > rule macro-F1; JEV accuracy rises with confidence; the agreement policy has higher accuracy on answered items than either system alone, at lower coverage.
E11.data: 59 records: COMPADRE source DOIs (labels from MatrixTreatment), audited study DOIs, OpenAlex works with chemistry/pharmacology/medicine primary topic; labels frozen 2026-11-07T21:45:39+00:00
E11.method: Rubric labels (not expert labels); abstentions count as not answered; no threshold tuned on this set.
E11.finding: Macro-F1: JEV 0.768, rules 0.773, LLM zero-shot (Groq/Gemini) 0.825 on 59. Agent policy: accuracy on answered 0.843 at coverage 0.864 (JEV alone 0.807 at 0.966). Rubric labels, n=59; JEV stays advisory. Run-to-run: JEV macro-F1 0.802 (run 1) vs 0.768 (run 2) on the same frozen labels; the hypothesis is not supported on the latest run.

E12.title: Survey planner benchmark: ILP vs greedy vs random vs top-suitability
E12.question: Under identical constraints (budget, no adjacent cells), does the exact ILP improve the stated survey objective over simple baselines, and does it respond monotonically to budget?
E12.hypothesis: ILP objective >= every baseline at every budget (by construction) with gains largest at larger budgets; objective is non-decreasing in budget; top-suitability covers fewer environmental strata.
E12.data: 3 regions x 4 budgets; WorldClim, Open-Meteo DEM, GBIF, habitat model where eligible
E12.finding: ILP >= all baselines in every case: True; budget-monotone: True. Median gain vs greedy 0.1% (max 5.9%), vs random 28.6%. Greedy is near-optimal at small budgets; gains are in the modelled objective, not demonstrated field outcomes.

E13.title: Evidence planning: complementarity-aware ILP vs item-greedy
E13.question: When decisions need ALL of several measurements (e.g. a local quota needs 6), does a greedy ranking of individual measurements waste budget compared with an ILP that models complementarity?
E13.hypothesis: Greedy buys individually attractive items that complete no decision at some budgets; ILP unlocks >= as much decision value at every budget.
E13.method: budgets 10..120 person-days; 4 species with different tiers
E13.finding: ILP >= greedy in all 24 cases; greedy strictly worse in 15 (mean value gap 1.34). Evidence planning must model 'all-of' requirements; the app uses the ILP and shows the greedy result for transparency.

E14.title: Khaya senegalensis stochastic growth: harvested vs unharvested (annual pooled matrices)
E14.question: Using COMPADRE's annual pooled matrices (2004-05, 2005-06), is stochastic lambda lower in high-harvest than unmanipulated populations, matching the direction reported by Gaoue & Ticktin?
E14.hypothesis: lambda_s(high harvest) < lambda_s(unmanipulated); only 2 annual matrices per arm so uncertainty is large.
E14.finding: Stochastic lambda high-harvest 0.9725 vs unmanipulated 0.9724 (difference +0.0001): the published harvest penalty is NOT reproduced from COMPADRE's two pooled annual matrices per arm; the paper's stochastic analysis used a different (ecoregion-specific, multi-year) structure.

E15.title: Data-quality sensitivity: do COMPADRE QC failures change medicinal-species conclusions?
E15.question: How many medicinal matrices fail QC (NA, survival>1, A!=U+F+C) and would including them shift species-level median lambda?
E15.hypothesis: <10% fail QC; species-level median lambda shifts <0.01 when failing matrices are excluded.
E15.finding: 15% of medicinal matrices fail at least one QC check (hypothesis <10% rejected). Median species-level lambda shift is 0.000, but 9 species shift >0.05 (survival>1 matrices can produce extreme lambda). Decision: QC-failing matrices are never used as Simulate presets.
